summary:
Nobody has measured how fire behaves on the Moon. A lunar habitat will run on more oxygen, lower pressure and one-sixth gravity, and all three change how a flame ignites, spreads and goes out. NASA has decades of combustion experiments in its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, but the evidence is scattered across tables, reports and slides.

Lunar Fire Atlas brings that evidence together in one tool. We extracted 1,115 observations and 1,283 citable text passages from 13 PSI investigations (ACME, FLEX, BASS, SAFFIRE and others). The Atlas has three parts: a 3D lab that shows the same flame side by side in microgravity, lunar and Earth gravity; an evidence map that places every real trial by oxygen and pressure, with links to its source; and an AI research copilot that answers questions with a verdict, the matching trials, exact citations and suggested next experiments. A verification layer with no AI checks every number and citation against NASA's data.

The key finding: all 1,115 observations were made in microgravity, and none in lunar gravity. The Atlas shows exactly where the missing experiments are, so they can be run before people live on the Moon.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Fire Atlas is a web tool that gathers what NASA knows about combustion beyond Earth, makes it explorable, and shows what still needs to be studied before people live on the Moon. A lunar habitat will likely use an atmosphere with more oxygen and lower pressure than Earth's (NASA's exploration atmosphere: 8.2 psia, 34% O2), under one-sixth gravity. All three factors change how a flame ignites, spreads and goes out. NASA has decades of fire experiments in its Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, but the results are spread across tables, reports and slides. To answer one concrete question, you have to read and compare several documents by hand.

HOW IT WORKS

We took 13 PSI combustion investigations flown on the ISS and on Cygnus spacecraft (ACME, FLEX, CFI, SAME, BASS, SAFFIRE and others) and turned their tables into 1,115 standardized observations. Each observation records the material, oxygen, pressure, gravity and outcome. We also split their reports into 1,283 text passages that can be searched and cited. The Atlas has three connected parts:

1. 3D comparative lab: pick a material, oxygen level and pressure, and watch the same flame side by side in microgravity, lunar gravity and Earth gravity. It shows qualitative trends and is labeled as illustrative, not as a predictive model.

2. Evidence map: places every real NASA trial on an oxygen-by-pressure chart, filters it by gravity, compares it with mission reference conditions (lunar and Martian habitats, the lunar EVA suit, the ISS cabin), and links each point to its original source.

3. Research copilot: answers natural-language questions with an "evidence brief": a verdict, a table of matching trials, exact citations, evidence gaps and suggested next experiments. Answers stream live, so you can watch each AI agent work.

KEY FINDING

All 1,115 observations were made in microgravity, and none in lunar gravity. For a lunar habitat, oxygen and pressure data are not what is missing. The effect of partial gravity has never been measured. The Atlas shows that gap and points to the experiments that would fill it.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners, researchers and students can answer in seconds questions that used to take hours of reading, and every answer traces back to its NASA source. The intended impact is to guide future partial-gravity fire-safety experiments and the choice of habitat materials and atmospheres for Artemis-era missions.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Three.js / React Three Fiber, D3, Tailwind CSS, GSAP, Motion, Zod, Vitest and Playwright, deployed on Vercel. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Pydantic, Claude Agent SDK, Voyage AI embeddings and reranking, and Pytest, deployed on Railway. Both sides follow Clean Architecture. No hardware was used.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a static dashboard, the Atlas tells a story: you change the flame, find the real trials, switch to lunar gravity, see an empty map, and ask the copilot what experiment is missing. The empty map is the finding itself.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty: the AI does not produce numbers. Filters and calculations run in Python over NASA data, and a verification layer that uses no AI checks every figure and citation, and drops anything that does not match. If the AI agents fail, the answer is built from fixed rules instead. Out-of-range trials are left off the map rather than moved to its edge, and the API reports how many were left out. Demo data is synthetic and labeled as such. Original NASA tables are kept unchanged. Credentials never reach the browser.
